articles.title: In the early 1900s, a United States plant explorer tested Japanese kudzu near Washington, D.C.; later promoted for soil protection, the “wonder plant” spread across millions of acres of the South
articles.summary: Kudzu was no accident of nature: federal agencies promoted it and paid for it, and the evidence shows an ecological impact that is real but smaller than
articles.body: Kudzu was no accident of nature: federal agencies promoted it and paid for it, and the evidence shows an ecological impact that is real but smaller than the legend suggests. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935 as a USDA agency and now known as the Natural Resources Conservation Service, tested, praised, and paid farmers to plant kudzu in the 1930s and 1940s, before the ecological cost was counted, as naturalist Bill Finch recounts in Smithsonian Magazine.David Fairchild planted kudzu seedlings around his home in 1902Kudzu first reached the United States as an ornamental vine in the Japanese pavilion at the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition of 1876. A paper from the USDA Forest Service Southern Research Station picks up the story from there. David Fairchild, the plant explorer, had seen farmers in Japan using kudzu for grazing, and in 1902 he planted kudzu seedlings in his garden near Washington, D.C., to see how the plant would behave. By 1907, kudzu hay had been demonstrated in Jamestown, Virginia, a sign of growing interest in the plant as livestock feed. Fairchild, however, grew wary of it. By 1938, he had turned against the plant, and in his autobiography, The World Was My Garden, he recalled firsthand how kudzu covered bushes and climbed pines, smothering them. That account reflects Fairchild's own experience with his experiment, not an official USDA position on kudzu.More than 1.2 million acres were planted after the Soil Conservation Service backed kudzuC. E. Pleas, a farmer from Chipley, Florida, discovered that livestock eagerly ate kudzu. After confirming with the USDA that the plant was not poisonous, he promoted it as a forage crop through newspaper articles and pamphlets, according to Florida Memory, the Florida Department of State's archive program. He turned into an avid fan of the crop and planted 35 acres to sell as fodder. In the 1930s and 1940s, the Soil Conservation Service promoted kudzu as a means of stabilizing soil in the rapidly eroded gullies of the South, particularly in the Piedmont regions of Alabama, Georgia, and Mississippi. The agency distributed more than 85 million seedlings and paid farmers to plant the vine. The farmers were paid to plant kudzu, and more than 1.2 million acres were planted under this federal program. This number covers only the acreage planted under the federal program, not all the kudzu planted in the U.S., and Bill Finch's reporting in Smithsonian Magazine puts total plantings at a little more than a million acres by 1945.Kudzu's growth rate rises with carbon dioxide, and it spends little on woody tissueWhy did the vine take so well? Kudzu (Pueraria montana): History, Physiology, and Ecology Combine to Make a Major Ecosystem Threat, published in Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences in 2004, offers part of the answer. The growth of kudzu is stimulated significantly by increased levels of CO₂, according to Irwin Forseth and Anne Innis of the University of Maryland, College Park. Because kudzu does not invest in woody structure, this growth boost could make it even more competitive as atmospheric CO₂ concentrations rise. A fast-growing plant that invests little in woody tissue can outcompete slower-growing rivals.Nitrogen fixation more than doubles nitric oxide emissions from invaded soilsThe plant also alters the soil it grows in. Jonathan Hickman and colleagues showed this in "Kudzu (Pueraria montana) Invasion Doubles Emissions of Nitric Oxide and Increases Ozone Pollution," published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2010. The authors point to the southeastern United States as an area of particular concern: because kudzu fixes nitrogen, it drives extra nitric oxide emissions from the soil, and nitric oxide feeds ozone formation. In 2007, the team studied soils at three sites in Madison County, Georgia. In invaded soils, net nitrogen mineralization rose by up to 1,000% and net nitrification by up to 500% compared with control soils, and nitric oxide emissions were more than 100% higher (2.81 versus 1.24 ng NO‑N cm⁻² h⁻¹). Only these figures are field measurements.The researchers then fed their data into the GEOS‑Chem atmospheric chemistry model and assumed an extreme scenario in which kudzu invaded all nonagricultural, nonurban soils across nine southeastern states. Under that scenario, soil nitric oxide emissions rose by 28%, and some areas saw up to seven additional days each summer when 8-hour ozone concentrations exceeded 70 ppb. These are projections, not measurements.Forest Service survey data puts kudzu on about 227,000 acres of Southern forestlandKudzu is often said to cover seven million to nine million acres of the United States, but Bill Finch, writing in Smithsonian Magazine's "The True Story of Kudzu, the Vine That Never Truly Ate the South," reports that scientists reassessing its spread found nothing close to that. Forest Service survey data from 2010 shows that 227,000 acres of southern forestland contain kudzu, about one-tenth of 1 percent of the region's 200 million acres of forestland. This estimate covers forestland only, so kudzu growing on other land is not counted.The Forest Service expects the infested forestland to grow by no more than 2,500 acres a year, while some sources repeat an unsupported figure of 150,000 acres a year. The research on kudzu's ecology helps explain why the plant competes so well. Forseth and Innis (2004) attribute kudzu's edge to two physiological traits: a fast response to high CO₂ concentrations and little investment in woody tissue. Much of what people say about kudzu's ecological effects comes from testimony rather than measurement, which is why the Forest Service survey and the studies above matter. It was planted deliberately, its growth habits give it a competitive edge, and its effects on soil chemistry reach as far as the air above it. Its environmental impact is smaller than some legends suggest.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Cuba tensions on the rise as Trump pushes for ‘fundamental change’
articles.summary: Tensions between the U.S. and Cuba are rising once again after President Trump told world leaders gathered at the United Nations General Assembly that he was seeking “fundamental change” from the island and asserting that “freedom will be coming to Cuba.” The Trump administration has never walked back threats of a possible military intervention —…
articles.body:
Tensions between the U.S. and Cuba are rising once again after President Trump told world leaders gathered at the United Nations General Assembly that he was seeking “fundamental change” from the island and asserting that “freedom will be coming to Cuba.”

The Trump administration has never walked back threats of a possible military intervention — an idea Cuban leaders were asked about this week after a report from CBS News .

The report included interviews with officials who said planning documents about sending Army Reserve staff to aid Southern Command, the Pentagon’s wing focused on the Caribbean, were in reference to Cuba.

Meanwhile, Cuban officials present for the General Assembly slammed Trump for calling them a “failed state.” They also criticized the U.S. for imposing a fuel blockade they say has crippled activity on the island — but not their resolve — as the U.S. pushes for regime change.

“A few days ago, the president of the United States declared in this room that Cuba was ‘a failed State’. If that were the case, why did they have to impose a fuel blockade? Why did they impose secondary sanctions? Why do they have to threaten, persecute and exert pressures on other states?” Cuba’s Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla said during Saturday’s speech .

“We are often asked what is the U.S. pursuing with such an aggressive behavior, and the question usually surprises us, because the representatives of that government have outrightly declared their purpose to take Cuba, control the country and dominate the economy.”

A U.S. blockade has choked off the oil supply to the island, and an already struggling electric grid is now largely nonfunctional, with power at most available for an hour or two each day.

Cuba has also rolled out a series of economic reforms long called for by U.S. officials. Though they represent a significant opening of Cuba’s economy, including to foreign investment, those measures come as the Trump administration continually rolls out punishing new sanctions, including to those seeking to do business in Cuba.

Francisco Pichón, a U.N. coordinator in Cuba, told The New York Times earlier this month that shipping companies carrying items not covered by sanctions — including food and medical supplies — were showing signs of “over-compliance,” failing to deliver allowed materials out of fear of running afoul of U.S. sanctions.

Throughout the week at the General Assembly, the Trump administration took jabs at Cuba.

Trump during a press conference referenced Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is Cuban American, in saying that he would “someday in the near future drop him off in the middle of Cuba.”

And though he mentioned Cuba briefly in his 37-minute address before the assembly, Trump’s comments were pointed.

“My administration is also seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba, where the communist regime is under great pressure — the biggest pressure they’ve ever been under. It’s an absolutely failed state. It’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” Trump said.

“Marco Rubio is handling a negotiation. He’s deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let’s see what happens.”

He accused Cuba of claims they’ve long denied of being a threat to the U.S. and also accused them, without evidence, of having “cultivated ties to subversive and radical groups such as the Communist Party USA, antifa, and the Democrat Socialists of America.”

“Communism will never be coming to America, but freedom will be coming to Cuba,” Trump said.

Rodríguez Parrilla rejected the idea that Cuba poses any threat to the U.S. and in an interview with NBC News denied any involvement in U.S. domestic affairs.

“Any minimally informed observer would understand the unrealistic and evil intention to portray a relatively small and developing nation like Cuba, with a modest economic performance, as a threat to the biggest nuclear, military, technological and economic power on the planet,” he said during his speech.

For months, U.S. and Cuban officials have been engaged in negotiations, including a February trip to St. Kitts for secret meetings.

Both sides have stayed mum about the contents of the discussions, but Rodríguez Parrilla told NBC, “They have not offered much progress or results.”

There are some outward signs that Cuba is pivoting amid U.S. pressure.

Cuba in June announced a sweeping package of 176 economic reforms that included significant measures to open its economy to foreign investment.

In its new reforms, Cuba reduced the number of industries where the private sector cannot operate. In addition to easing pathways for foreign investment in private industries, they also removed the cap — previously set at 100 — on how many employees private businesses could hire.

Ricardo Torres, a Cuban economist who is now a fellow at American University, said while the reforms are “quite ambitious,” the issue is timing.

“Many of those things have been discussed in Cuba for years, and the government always refused to implement them, to adopt them, and so it took an oil embargo and several executive orders from the U.S. to create the incentive for them to adopt that,” he told The Hill.

“The moment for Cuba to change successfully, relying basically on its own domestic reform, is gone. Now, given the severity of the crisis that the country is seeing and the lack of meaningful international support, some sanctions relief will be needed, and U.S. participation one way or the other will be needed. Because foreign capital or private capital is not going to go to Cuba under these sanctions. It’s too risky and Cuba is such a small market, so the timing is not good.”

It’s unclear the extent Cuba is embracing the reforms – and how long they plan to keep them.

In an interview with Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel called the reforms “necessary” even as he also called them a concession.

“For us, expanding the private sector is not an ideal of socialism. It is a concession,” he told the news outlet in the August interview.

He later added that the process would not be one that leads to “the restoration of capitalism,” asserting that the communist party that has run the country since 1959 still has the backing of the people.

Rubio has complained that Cuba has a credibility problem.

“Why would I invest $10 million in Cuba if two years from now they just decide on their own to change the rules, take it from me, and keep the money and never pay me back? And that’s happened over and over and over in Cuba. Even now, as they announce these reforms, everyone’s saying, ‘Well, these things are just on paper.’ A, you have to implement them, and B, you have to keep them,” he said during a press conference last week while attending the assembly.

“So certainty is the problem, and there’s simply no legitimacy or credibility that this regime will ever live up to these conditions because they never have before.”

Torres said Díaz-Canel was presenting a contradiction.

“You have a government presiding over a sinking economy — well, a collapsing country essentially — that is adopting proposals. They say that they want to attract foreign capital, that they want to expand the footprint of a private sector. Now, at the same time, the president is saying those are concessions. There is a big difference,” he said.

“Because if you say that it is a concession, you are saying that you are not committed to that, that you are not convinced that that is the way to go. You are saying that it’s a concession because you didn’t have any choice.”

During his interview with NBC, Rodríguez Parrilla repeatedly stressed that Cuba was not a threat to the U.S. and accused the Trump administration of a policy of “hunger, desperation, and the overthrowing of governments.”

“We are always preparing for any kind of situation. We have adopted measures to increase our defensive capability with the participation of the entire people,” he said when asked about the risk of the U.S. attack. “But the U.S. government will never be able to find any justification or reason to launch a military attack against a small neighboring country.”

articles.title: Trump, China and the question of selling arms to Beijing
articles.summary: Questions about whether the U.S. could change its posture toward China are on the rise after David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, made waves by saying President Trump had asked Chinese President Xi Jinping if he would “like to buy some.” The president on Monday denied making the offer to Xi, while close observers…
articles.body:
Questions about whether the U.S. could change its posture toward China are on the rise after David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, made waves by saying President Trump had asked Chinese President Xi Jinping if he would “like to buy some.”

The president on Monday denied making the offer to Xi, while close observers of the U.S.-China security competition warned the proposal would mark an extraordinary break with decades of American policy.

Many lawmakers and experts in Washington see China as Washington’s greatest diplomatic and economic adversary. Arms sales to China currently are illegal and a U.S. official told The Hill that the U.S. government has no plans to sell weapons to Beijing.

“It would require overcoming existing legal restrictions, raise obvious concerns about transferring sensitive U.S. military technology to America’s principal strategic competitor and scramble longstanding assumptions about U.S. security policy in the Indo-Pacific,” Craig Singleton, senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told The Hill on Monday.

“But given the State Department’s clarification that there is no offer or plan to sell weapons to China, I think the remark is more revealing as a window into Trump’s worldview than as an executable policy proposal,” he added.

Lyle Goldstein, the director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities, said Trump might have misspoken or made an offer “without thinking it through,” but logically many would be concerned about U.S. military technology going to Beijing. He noted that in the 1980s, China was considered an emerging market for U.S. weapons as Washington sold Blackhawk helicopters and lightweight torpedoes.

“These are both important weapons systems. In both cases, they helped the PLA make major advances. The huge role of the Blackhawk sale back then is reflected in the fact that the contemporary Z-20 that China is building in large numbers is derivative of the original American design,” he told The Hill on Monday, referring to the Harbin Z-20 medium-lift utility helicopter.

Goldstein said even if it’s impossible for the U.S. to sell high-end exquisite weapons systems, such as PAC-3 interceptors or Tomahawk missiles, it might be possible to sell Beijing “lower-end items.”

“If one takes the position that the U.S. and China are unlikely to go to war for many reasons, such as nuclear weapons and economic interdependence, then it becomes conceivable that they might actually offer mutual assistance and even engage in some trade in weapons for mutual benefit,” Goldstein said.

The Hill has reached out to the State Department for comment.

Trump seemed surprised when asked about his ambassador to China’s comments Monday.

“I never heard of that one,” he told reporters . “I’ll have to ask him.”

“They probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than them,” the president continued. “So maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss it.”

Trump said he thinks Perdue was talking about Taiwan in his comments.

The potential sale would unsettle U.S. allies in the region, including Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines, which all have boosted their defense spending as regional tensions have increased.

The U.S. announced a more than $11 billion arms sale to Taiwan last December. But a current $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan has been on hold for months and cannot move forward until the commander in chief formally transmits it to Congress.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said earlier this year that the pause is because of the U.S. war with Iran.

“There are many questions about this that only the President can answer. But there’s one potential arms sale that’s actually worth his support and also good for U.S. interests and that’s the $14 billion package for Taiwan that has been stalled for almost a year,” Chris Estep, a former U.S. official and an Indo-Pacific security expert with the Foreign Policy Research Institute, told The Hill on Monday.

“As China continues with the largest military buildup since World War II, U.S. allies and partners across the Indo-Pacific are stepping up by spending more on their own ability to defend themselves,” he said. “Washington should be focused on supporting their efforts instead.”

Trump said in May that he discussed the $14 billion Taiwan weapons package with Xi and called the arms deal a “very good negotiating chip” with Beijing.

Purdue did say in his interview that Trump “is as strong on Taiwan as I’ve ever seen anybody.”

“He’s made it very clear that we have not changed the one China policy,” he said. “We support the Taiwan Relations Act.”

Prior to Xi’s visit to Washington, Republican senators pressed the Trump administration to advance the massive arms package, along with other national security assistance to Taiwan.

“It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence in the Indo-Pacific if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities,” the senators wrote in a two-page letter.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that U.S. arms sales to Taiwan are in part limited by Washington’s potential defense needs in other corners of the world and the industrial base.

“People think … we view arm sales through the limited vacuum of the one particular place. A lot of this also involves balancing our industrial capacity and our military industrial base,” Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters last week.

Singleton, of FDD, said Perdue’s comments capture the president’s “highly transactional approach,” viewing tariffs, markets and weapons as instruments of leverage and dealmaking, “sometimes compressing the traditional distinction between allies and adversaries into the same negotiating frame.”

“In Perdue’s telling, Trump appears to have been trying to normalize U.S. arms sales by essentially saying: America sells weapons around the world, so why should this particular transaction be treated differently,” he said.

Normalizing arms sales matters because China views U.S. arms sales to Taiwan as a redline and a constraint on future U.S. behavior in the region, according to Singleton, a former U.S. diplomat.

“Trump may believe keeping the issue fluid preserves maximum flexibility. Beijing may interpret that fluidity as an opening to negotiate limits on future sales. That gap in expectations is potentially more consequential than the weapons remark itself.”

Andrew Harding, who served as special assistant for Asia on the National Security Council last year, said he thought Perdue’s comment was “interesting” but said he viewed it as a “nothing burger.”

“I don’t think this is a serious proposal because if it were, I would have expected to see more of it come out during the summit or as part of the White House deliverables,” Harding, currently a policy analyst for national security and Indo-Pacific affairs at the Heritage Foundation, told The Hill.

“I don’t expect to see any serious movement on that proposal … I think I’m more focused on the tangible issues in the relationship that China is not fully following through on, whether it’s on rare earth trade and watching to see how the White House preserves American leverage on these issues while holding China accountable.”

Goldstein, who is also a senior fellow at the Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs at Brown University, said it is possible that Trump is making an effort to lower the “level of mutual suspicion” between the countries and slash the trade deficit by selling older weaponry.

“Remember, it’s clear that Trump prioritizes the success of American companies and especially exports. His singular achievement in the Russia-Ukraine War has been to reduce America’s role, while continuing the process of U.S. weapons exports by getting the Europeans to fund these outlays,” he said. “It’s hard to imagine, but he could attempt to reduce the yawning trade deficit with China by selling them old American weapons.”

“I think the national security establishment would strongly oppose that approach, but Trump has questioned many orthodoxies in Washington,” Goldstein said.

articles.title: Council of Europe head revives Biden-backed framework for AI regulation
articles.summary: The Biden administration and a number of countries in Europe have endorsed a framework for AI regulation that respects human rights, democracy and the rule of law, but it is generally unheard of outside of the little-known European organization that drafted it. Alain Berset is the secretary-general of the Council of Europe, an important but…
articles.body:
The Biden administration and a number of countries in Europe have endorsed a framework for AI regulation that respects human rights, democracy and the rule of law, but it is generally unheard of outside of the little-known European organization that drafted it.

Alain Berset is the secretary-general of the Council of Europe, an important but relatively unknown independent organization of 46 member states and based in Strasbourg, France.

Berset, a former president of Switzerland, is trying to change that and bring some attention to his organization. He carried out an inaugural visit to Washington, D.C., last week and met with lawmakers on Capitol Hill, think tanks and journalists.

Part of his message was promoting the Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, a treaty published in September 2024 that was signed by the former Biden administration along with 20 other countries, including Japan and Israel, as well as a number of countries in Europe and the Americas.

The framework is a legally-binding document but has only been ratified, so far, by the European Union — and only recently, in May 2026.

But President Trump’s rejection and criticism of any regulation surrounding AI represents one of the biggest hurdles toward trying to convince other countries to take seriously dire warnings from tech companies and others about the destructive power of the advancing technology.

“I do not see any alternative to a strong, I would say, involvement of states,” Berset said when asked about the challenge of rallying international cooperation in what is generally viewed as a major arms race.

He argues the framework, already drafted and agreed, provides a starting point.

“For the first time, we have specialists telling us that this revolution could destroy humanity in a few years. This should be a quite hard wake up call for all of us, to say, ‘OK, what do we propose for this?’ … And the framework convention is exactly that,” he said.

Berset’s advocacy in Washington, D.C., came after a stop in New York to the United Nations General Assembly, where the Council of Europe opened a permanent observer office to the U.N.

The point of the office is to expose the council to a larger audience and raise the visibility of its work on human rights, democracy and the rule of law — with AI being a dominant topic.

Last week, AI leaders urged the United Nations Security Council to put restraints on their companies , warning of a real and imminent threat to humanity.

The global reach provided by the U.N. presents an important venue for the council to promote its Framework on AI, providing a structure grounded in human rights, democracy and rule of law, Berset said at the opening of the council’s office at the U.N.

“Our task is to connect these strengths,” he said.

The council is one of Europe’s oldest human rights organizations, created in 1949 in the aftermath of World War II and the horrors of the Holocaust. One of the first treaties established by the council was the European Convention on Human Rights, a legally binding document enforced by the European Court of Human Rights.

The council has drafted approximately 200 treaties, and Berset said the court has taken one million decisions — making it a valuable resource for justice, accountability and resolution.

What also makes the council unique is that membership is not limited to European Union member countries. Its 46 member states also include aspiring EU-countries, like Turkey and Ukraine, and observer states like the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan and the Holy See.

“We have created the biggest common legal space that exists in the world,” Berset said in a speech at the Hudson Institute.

“It’s not that visible but it’s extremely important for having this convergence, year after year, between the 46 members of the council of Europe.”

The council’s large membership and history in treaty drafting, pursuit of ratification and enforcement mechanisms make it a good starting point for conversations on AI, Berset argues.

“I think it is one contribution. It is not the only one, it will not be the only one, but it is one concrete contribution,” he told The Hill.

To naysayers against the Framework on AI, he urges other creative ideas but not to dismiss what has already been accomplished.

“I would be more than happy if you bring a better answer. We have at least one answer, we have one element. We have one framework where we are able to work together to follow this,” Berset said.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Burnham opens debate on huge issue of social care reform
articles.summary: The pitch from Andy Burnham is that there needs to be a willingness to say "the things politicians usually avoid", the BBC's political editor writes.
articles.body:
Conference speech day is always a big day for a prime minister, and perhaps no bigger than when it is your first one in the role.

The pitch from Andy Burnham is that "hope comes from honesty," there needs to be "less drift and more direction" and there needs to be a willingness to say "the things politicians usually avoid."

On Sunday, he told the BBC he wants to shake up social care in England , but would only be able to do so after a general election given he was committed to the tax promises Sir Keir Starmer made at the last general election.

This prompted a flurry of chat about how his social care plan could be paid for - and in particular the future of what is known as the triple lock, the promise to increase the state pension in line with wages, prices or 2.5%, whichever is the highest.

But plenty of politicians, in multiple parties, have long privately fretted that its cost is ballooning and will continue to do so, but would bemoan how politically difficult it would be to drop it.

It's a tricky one for the prime minister: he has the leader of the Unite union, Sharon Graham, saying it could be "electoral suicide" to ditch the triple lock.

Meanwhile the markets - which determine the cost of borrowing for the government - are keeping a keen eye on whether Burnham's promises appear to be financially credible.

In other words, he has to be able to point to things where money won't be spent, as well as where it will be.

No10 are being pretty coy about precisely what Andy Burnham will or won't say on all this later on.

They really don't want to overcook it or overdo it, instead suggesting it is others who have been getting carried away.

But ministers are well aware that a hare is running about it all - and given that, it would be extraordinary if there was no mention of it all, given that promise about "honesty," candour and trade offs.

Sufficiently extraordinary that his critics would pounce on what they'd see as a precise lack of the very thing he is promising - candour.

Why the PM could finally drop the triple lock pension pledge

Burnham to unveil public body to invest in electricity grid

Folk I am hearing from this morning suggest, as one figure put it, "people will be surprised on the upside" about how much Burnham will be willing to lean into the options that could be explored as part of Labour's offer at the next general election.

He will be explicit it will be retained, as promised, until the election.

Instead, it would appear Burnham will seek to seed a conversation about all of the above, without nailing down the details.

His allies see this as a different approach to politics – being open about options, starting a debate but not crudely or abruptly shifting policy.

There is an implicit comparison with Sir Keir Starmer's ditching of the Winter Fuel Payment – which appeared to come from nowhere and had a near immediate impact.

But that didn't stop Graham likening the two approaches – claiming "the danger of doing it" is that Labour could "waste" a second hearing which it now has under Andy Burnham.

In the round, though, ministers I speak to are relishing what they see as a return to big arguments, about generational issues with a prime minister willing to wrestle with them in public.

This afternoon we will get a fuller sense of the scope and scale of that – on social care, pensions and much else.

articles.title: Celine Dion kicks off Paris Fashion Week with I'm Alive performance under Eiffel Tower
articles.summary: The singer appeared at the end of L'Oreal's annual show as the French fashion bonanza kicked off.
articles.body:
Celine Dion has opened Paris Fashion Week with a surprise performance of her 2002 hit I'm Alive, underneath the city's famous Eiffel Tower.

The Canadian star, who was diagnosed with a rare neurological disease called stiff person syndrome in 2022, took to the runway at the end of L'Oreal's annual show.

The singer, who wore a ruched full-length velvet black gown, was later joined by famous ambassadors for the French brand, including Viola Davis, Simone Ashley, Aja Naomi King and Eva Longoria.

Dion recently performed a comeback show in the city earlier this month, her first since her 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short.

Paris Fashion Week, showcasing women's spring/summer collections, runs until 6 October.

Actress Viola Davis was feeling the love from the crowd as she joined Dion under the stars in the French capital.

Kendall Jenner also modelled at the show, wearing a sheer black halterneck dress with thigh split and an ivory corset underneath.

Supermodel Cara Delavingne, meanwhile, walked the runway in a sparkling red sheer dress with train.

Pop star Rihanna brought her usual fashion credentials to Paris on day one, with a shimmering, glamorous copper two-piece worn over sheer black lingerie.

She was on the front row of the Matières Fécales fashion show - the label behind Zendaya's angel wings dress at The Odyssey premiere in New York this summer.

Wicked star Cynthia Erivo was also in the French capital at a Tiffany and M.A.D - Musée des Arts Décoratifs - event.

Other labels showing in Paris over the next week include Louis Vuitton, Tom Ford, Schiaparelli, Givenchy, Jean Paul Gaultier, Balenciaga and Loewe.

The fashion world is keeping a particularly close eye on Dior and Chanel, after both signed up new artistic directors last year.

Matthieu Blazy took over as Chanel's creative director in early 2025, while Jonathan Anderson began the same role at Dior last summer.

This week should see the pair continue to solidify their strategies for the two brands. Expect some serious aesthetic rivalry on the runways.

articles.title: Why has a Cornell rape investigation been reopened?
articles.summary: Former student at Ivy League university files lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
articles.body:
New York state prosecutors have reopened a case involving an alleged gang rape at Cornell University after a woman filed a civil lawsuit accusing the school and law enforcement officials of not doing enough.

According to court documents filed in the lawsuit on September 16, which include screenshots of a group chat purportedly between members of the university fraternity at the centre of the allegations, the woman, referred to as Jane Doe, alleged she was drugged and raped at the fraternity house in 2024.

The case has sparked anger on social media directed at Cornell and the District Attorney’s Office in Tompkins County, New York, over their handling of the allegations.

On Monday, District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said in a statement that while at the time of the assault his office had found that evidence from the complainant’s initial statement did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges, he would now let a grand jury decide.

“Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available – by testimony to the Tompkins County grand jury,” Van Houten said.

According to the 101-page lawsuit, the complainant visited a friend at the Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, on October 19, 2024, while she was already intoxicated after drinking at a local, off-campus bar.

She stated that two members of the house propositioned her to sleep with both of them and later pressured her into taking ketamine and smoking marijuana.

Doe, 20 at the time, alleged she was then raped by seven men at the Chi Phi fraternity house over the course of seven hours before blacking out about 5:45am.

She said in the lawsuit that because she was under the influence, there was no way she was able to provide consent.

Doe added that although she reported the incident to the university’s police department on November 8, 2024, prosecutors filed no criminal charges.

In a statement to US broadcaster CBS News on Monday, Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said she went to the police because she believed she was the “victim of a crime”.

“Other than her initial contact with Cornell Police, she was not contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors,” Giuffra said.

He added that Cornell expelled two fraternity members after an internal review of the allegations, but five others received lesser repercussions, including suspensions, workshops and essay assignments.

“Not one of these guys was arrested. Not one. That I can tell you for a fact,” Giuffra told CBS New York, adding that Doe dropped out of school after her ordeal.

The lawsuit names Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar as the men in question.

It also names Cornell; the Chi Phi fraternity; Doe’s sorority, Delta Delta Delta; the off-campus bar; and the seven men as defendants and accuses them of breach of contract, negligence and violations of state law.

Doe is seeking monetary damages, including compensatory and punitive damages. The lawsuit did not specify how much Doe was asking for.

The lawsuit includes images of a group chat on Snapchat among members of the fraternity in which one person alerted others crudely that they could sleep with the victim for “free”.

An image of the group chat shows a message from one person who wrote: “I f****** love Chi Phi.”

Kretzschmar, a then-fraternity member, allegedly sent two responses in the Snapchat group but has denied involvement.

Yes. Kretzschmar’s attorney, Jeremy Saland, told CBS News that the messages were inappropriate but were not evidence of sexual assault.

“This is a situation where there was an ugly Snapchat – ugly, period. … But that doesn’t make my client a rapist, and it certainly doesn’t make anyone a sex offender,” Saland said.

He added that his client had briefly entered the room where Doe was but did not touch her “in any way, shape or form” and left quickly afterwards.

Regarding the accusation of ketamine use, Saland said Kretzschmar took a hair follicle test that found he did not have the drug in his system, adding that no one has contacted him about a renewed investigation.

“We are available to present exonerating evidence. I just hope the right thing is eventually done, this case is closed and my client can live his life and not be subject to this selfish, repugnant, vile claim by this woman about him,” he added.

Meanwhile, Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney representing Lopes, also told CBS New York that his client “unequivocally denies the allegations against him”.

In a statement published on Monday, Cornell said it supports the district attorney’s decision to have Doe’s story heard by a grand jury.

It explained that the university initially conducted its own investigation into the allegations over several months and sent the matter to a hearing in which a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence from Doe and the defendants.

“At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement,” the statement read, adding that Chi Phi fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

“Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false. A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault,” it added.

According to Van Houten’s statement on Monday, in Doe’s initial statement in November 2024, she did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped.

“On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later,” he said.

“I recognise the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them. Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” the statement added.

Van Houten said a female senior prosecutor from his office who has significant experience in prosecuting sex crimes and has been involved in conducting jury trials in college sexual assault cases will prepare the case for the grand jury.

How common is sexual assault on university campuses in the US?

According to the Association of American Universities Campus Climate Survey in 2019, the overall rate of nonconsensual sexual contact by physical force or an inability to consent among women attending universities in the United States was 13 percent.

Among undergraduate women, the rate was 26.4 percent, or roughly one in four students. For undergraduate men, it was 6.9 percent.

Among postgraduate female students, 10.8 percent reported sexual contact by physical force or an inability to consent.

articles.title: Don’t let our next UN secretary-general be a shill for China, Cuba and Hamas
articles.summary: The U.S. has good reason to doubt the suitability of Rodrigues-Birkett, who with good reason appears likely to get China’s endorsement.
articles.body:
The race to choose the next U.N. secretary-general has yet to produce a clear frontrunner, but at least one candidate currently making headway should ring alarm bells in Washington.

The most recent straw poll of U.N. Security Council members showed Rebeca Grynspan , a former Costa Rican vice-president who has led the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development since 2021, with a razor-thin lead. But right behind her was Guyana’s current ambassador to the U.N., Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, who had led in the previous straw poll.

To win the position, a successful candidate needs the backing of nine of the 15 members of the council while avoiding the vetoes of any of its five permanent members — the U.S., China, the United Kingdom, France and Russia.

The U.S. has good reason to doubt the suitability of Rodrigues-Birkett, who will be stepping up her efforts to win the post, especially as several world leaders said at the recent U.N. General Assembly that they wanted to see a woman at the helm of the U.N. Although Guyana is a U.S. ally, Rodrigues-Birkett’s positions are more aligned with the Chinese Communist Party, the Cuban regime and Hamas than the U.S. and its closest allies. Indeed, China — Washington’s principal global adversary — appears likely to endorse her.

Amid an increasingly torrid domestic debate about the regulation of Artificial Intelligence, Rodrigues-Birkett has endorsed China’s newly launched World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization. Among the 29 members who signed this organization’s founding agreement, you will find such authoritarian U.S. adversaries as Russia, Cuba and Nicaragua. At a time when the U.S. is attempting to maintain dominance in the AI sector as well as deal with its social challenges, it certainly does not need a UN Secretary General in China’s pocket on this question — or, indeed, on others.

Rodrigues-Birkett’s affinity for China was on full display when took her campaign to Beijing in July. While four other hopefuls also visited the Chinese capital, she was the only one to support explicitly the 1971 U.N. General Assembly resolution recognizing the People’s Republic of China as “the only legitimate representatives of China to the United Nations.” China’s communist regime routinely invokes this resolution to justify shutting democratic Taiwan out of the U.N. system entirely. Washington has consistently rejected China’s contention that the resolution bars Taiwan from meaningful participation in international organizations.

Additionally, China’s official readout noted that Rodrigues-Birkett “spoke highly of the four major global initiatives proposed by China.” Those four initiatives — on development, security, civilization and global governance — are central pillars of President Xi Jinping’s effort to recast the rules and institutions of international cooperation in ways that serve Beijing.

Rodrigues-Birkett has also been a supporter of a communist regime in our own hemisphere. In a 2013 speech, she lauded the late dictator Fidel Castro, who imposed Soviet-style communism on Cuba, as a “visionary, determined revolutionary.” In the same year, while serving as Guyana’s foreign minister, she sponsored a motion in that country’s National Assembly condemning the U.S. blockade of Cuba. In a related interview, she claimed that Cuba — which has imprisoned thousands of dissidents, punishing their families in many cases as well, as one would expect from a totalitarian regime — “has been kind to everyone.”

Concerns about Rodrigues-Birkett extend to her views on the war in Gaza, too. In the aftermath of Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023 massacre in southern Israel, she paid lip service to the plight of the abducted hostages but squarely placed the blame for the escalating conflict on Israel, accusing Jerusalem of executing a “ veritable genocide .”

She has also pushed aggressively for the continued involvement in postwar Gaza of the U.N. Relief and Works Agency — the U.N. refugee agency dedicated solely to Palestinians. The U.S. has called for the agency’s abolition because as many as 100 of its then-current or former employees allegedly participated in the Ham a s atrocities , and because the inspector general for USAID is investigating alleged links to terrorism by as many as 1,500 of its current and former employees .

The U.S. needs a U.N. Secretary General who will support the success of President Trump’s plan to stabilize Gaza by pressing for the disarmament of Hamas, rather than amplifying its propaganda while defending a U.N. agency that has provided the terrorists with material support.

As a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, the U.S. can veto a recommendation to elect Rodrigues-Birkett. It should do so, even if that comes with protests back in Guyana. Richard Goldberg is a Senior Advisor to the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, where Ben Cohen is a Research Fellow.

articles.title: Trump administration ban on $1B in Canadian imports goes into effect
articles.summary: President Trump’s ban on nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian goods went into effect Tuesday, marking the latest salvo in a trade war between the U.S. and its longtime ally to the north. The restrictions include Canadian dairy products, motor vehicles and many alcoholic beverages. Trump, in signing the executive orders to ban the goods,…
articles.body:
President Trump’s ban on nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian goods went into effect Tuesday, marking the latest salvo in a trade war between the U.S. and its longtime ally to the north.

The restrictions include Canadian dairy products, motor vehicles and many alcoholic beverages. Trump, in signing the executive orders to ban the goods , cited Canadian “discrimination” against the American equivalents .

Jacob Jensen, the director of trade policy at the center-right American Action Forum, told The Associated Press the limits cover $967 million worth of Canadian imports, based on 2025 data.

Last year, U.S. businesses imported roughly $382 billion worth of goods from Canada, according to data from the U.S. Census Bureau.

The president last month slapped 50 percent tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian products, levies that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government matched “dollar for dollar.”

Trump justified his latest action under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which gives the U.S. government authority to block the importation of certain products if the president determines a foreign country has discriminated against American commerce.

He has repeatedly attacked Carney and Ottawa amid the trade tensions , saying Monday the Canadian government has “treated the U.S. very unfairly” by charging American businesses for exports.

“They have been one of the worst countries in the entire world,” the president told reporters in the Oval Office, later adding Canadian officials “feel entitled.”

Carney, meanwhile, has used the trade dispute with Trump to shift his country’s cooperative focus elsewhere.

During an address to the European Parliament earlier this month, the second-year prime minister said his country and Europe are “stronger together.”

“We can ally by function, if we are bold and deliberate,” he said, a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen backed adding Canada as the European Union’s first associate member.

articles.title: Florida is set to execute a 77-year-old man convicted of a 1995 murder
articles.summary: Curtis Wilkie Beasley was convicted of beating a woman to death with a hammer and is scheduled Tuesday to become the 16th person executed this year in the nation’s busiest death chamber.
articles.body: MIAMI — A 77-year-old Florida man convicted of beating a woman to death with a hammer is scheduled Tuesday to become the 16th person executed this year in the nation’s busiest death chamber. Curtis Wilkie Beasley was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder, robbery and grand theft auto in a 1995 attack on Carolyn Monfort. The Florida Supreme Court last week rejected appeals that executing a man his age who is suffering from cognitive decline would amount to cruel and unusual punishment. Beasley, who would become Florida’s seventh prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, is set to receive a three-drug injection at the state prison starting at 6 p.m. It was one of two executions scheduled this week in the U.S. Tennessee plans to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years on Wednesday by administering a lethal injection to Christa Pike, 50, who was convicted of killing a classmate in a jealous rage when they were both teens. Arrested while working under a fake name According to court records, Beasley had been staying at Monfort’s Dundee home, south of Orlando, in August 1995 while he was pressure washing and painting nearby apartments owned by her son-in-law. Monfort’s daughter went to her home after being unable to reach her for two days and found her body in a blood-splattered laundry room. Monfort suffered multiple blunt-force trauma injuries to the head, and a bloody hammer head was found wrapped in a towel nearby, according to investigators. Authorities began searching for Beasley after a witness reported seeing him driving what turned out to be Monfort’s car. Investigators determined Beasley had traveled to Miami and later relocated to Alabama, where he was arrested while working under a fake name for an electrical company, officials said. Beasley was convicted of murder and sentenced to death in 1998. A final appeal remains pending before the U.S. Supreme Court. Florida has carried out more than half of the nation’s executions this year Beasley would be the nation’s 29th execution this year, most of which have taken place in Florida. The state is getting closer to last year’s 19 executions, which was a record in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Two more are scheduled for this year, but Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has temporarily paused the next one. William Lee Thompson, 74, is scheduled to be executed Oct. 13 over raping and fatally beating a woman at a Florida motel in 1976. After a doctor this month determined Thompson might be suffering from dementia, DeSantis ordered a panel of three psychiatrists to examine him Thursday to determine if he is competent to be executed. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, issued similar stays in 2023 and 2025 but both executions proceeded following evaluations. William Reaves, 77, has an Oct. 20 execution date. He was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy outside a convenience store in 1986. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

articles.title: On Iran, Greenland and press access, Trump is more talk than action
articles.summary: The administration of Donald Trump is a tale told by an autocrat “full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.”
articles.body:
The Trump administration is a tale told by an autocrat “ full of sound and fury, signifying nothing .”

President Trump seemingly operates on whim and caprice, with little deference to Congress or the Constitution. Last April, he threatened to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages.” Nothing happened.

Last week at the United Nations, he conjured the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev, brandishing his shoe and banging it on a desk in 1960 while openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow U.N. member state. Trump announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran.

Trump told Iran to make a deal or be destroyed. “Will a deal be made with Iran?” he asked . “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

Both the message and the forum he chose to deliver it are regrettable.

Trump’s threats were emptier than Khruschev’s shoe-banging. Dictator Khruschev didn’t need anyone’s consent to bury us. But Trump does, and he is unlikely to get it. Earlier this month, the House voted to pass a resolution to end the war. A growing number of Republicans joined Democrats in favor of the resolution.

Trump can turn on a dime. In 2025, he announced he would annex Greenland. This year, he refused to rule out the use of military force for this annexation and threatened a 25 percent tariff on several European nations unless Denmark ceded Greenland to the U.S.

Last week at the U.N., he scrapped his bid for annexation and signed a new deal including Denmark, which experts said was largely identical to the existing 1951 deal giving the U.S. carte blanche to build new military bases on Greenland. The new deal has a kicker providing in substance it is only operative so long as the U.S. is a member of NATO .

Trump despises congressional oversight, and obtaining consent of Congress has never been one of his easy virtues. He has sought to justify a 90,000 square foot ballroom where the east wing of the White House used to be — without congressional consent — on the spurious basis that he needs to add a backyard bunker to improve White House security. He forgot to mention that we have a bunker there already .

He reportedly admitted that the ballroom is “a monument. I’m building a monument to myself — because no one else will.”

Recycling the shopworn national security argument, he seeks to construct an Arc de Trump that has been trashed by architects and architectural experts for its “super-size Las Vegas vulgarity.” Realizing that he needs the consent of Congress to take such a calamitous step, he now rebrands the project as essential defense infrastructure , seeking to place in the arch launching pads for drones and sniper nests.

Critics slammed the far-fetched proposal, pointing out that placing a drone launching pad directly underneath the primary landing path for Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport menaces navigation. Can you imagine the announcement as your plane descends towards Washington? “Attention all passengers, this is the captain. We have to divert to Philadelphia. Our flight path is infested with drones.”

Then there is the Constitution. In the most unconstitutional thing Trump has done since taking office, he banned without notice or hearing CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds, claiming they had been guilty of years of false reporting . In a curt White House statement , he contended that the First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat or place in the press pool.

The move sparked a lawsuit which Trump said he expects to lose in the district court. He also triggered a unified TV network boycott.

In court papers arguing for the ban, Attorney General Todd Blanche made the extraordinary argument that removing the three channels’ access to the White House was within the president’s discretion. Access to the news is “a privilege, not a right,” the government argued, adding that their presence poses a threat to national security by “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods.”

Not so, responded, federal Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee. Kelly issued a 14-day restraining order directing the White House to restore the journalists’ credentials. He ruled the ban was likely unconstitutional as denying the outlets’ due process rights.

In his early comments about the case, Trump focused not on national security but on negative coverage by the outlets and allegations of “ FAKE NEWS! ”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

In other words, he didn’t like the coverage.

Kelly appeared to be skeptical that Trump’s revocation of the journalists’ passes was truly motivated by national security. In the Pentagon Papers case , Justice Black overruled arguments about threats to national security, noting that the First Amendment “gave the free press the protection it must have to fulfill its essential role in our democracy.”

“The press was to serve the governed, not the governors.The government’s power to censor the press was abolished so that the press would remain forever free to censure the government.”

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: Post-Assad Syria is facing its biggest stress test yet. Here’s why that matters
articles.summary: This month, thousands of Syrians poured into the streets in the broadest protests since al-Assad’s fall. Unlike under his family’s 54-year police state, they were allowed to go home.
articles.body: In eastern Syria, a man complaining about soaring fuel prices turns to the crowd recording him on their phones and addresses the country’s transitional president. “We stood with you, so stand with us,” he shouts. “I swear by God, if things don’t change between now and the new year, the situation will turn into something we won’t want. Enough!” Security officers stand by as he openly denounces the government. What happens next is striking: nothing. Earlier this month, thousands of Syrians poured into the streets in the broadest protests since Bashar al-Assad’s fall nearly two years ago. Unlike under his family’s 54-year police state – where public defiance could mean prison, torture, disappearance or death – they were allowed to go home. The protests were widely broadcast on state media, in sharp contrast to Assad’s days, when state television peddled disinformation to discredit them, including claims that the protests were staged from faraway studios in Qatar. Syria is now navigating the gap between newfound political freedom and an economic recovery that remains frustratingly distant for ordinary citizens, many of whom are losing patience. The recent demonstrations were sparked by the government’s sudden decision to raise fuel prices by as much as 40%, which it blamed on the global energy crisis caused by the Iran war. As the outrage grew, the government walked back some increases and sent the energy minister before parliament in a show of accountability. Analysts have praised the government’s responsiveness to its biggest economic stress test yet, but warned it will not change the fundamentals of the country’s cost-of-living crisis. The World Bank assesses that two-thirds of Syrians live below the lower middle-income poverty line, on less than $3.65 a day. “We’re going to see these protests happening over and over again. It’s virtually impossible to overcome these severe economic challenges that Syrians are suffering. It will gradually become more challenging,” Ibrahim al-Assil, director of the Harvard Kennedy School’s Syria in Transition Lab, told CNN. That economic strain is causing a growing disconnect between Syrians’ expectations of their new government and their reality. “The honeymoon period was always going to come to an end. People’s expectations were going to rise, and their patience was going to wear thin if those expectations weren’t met. That’s basically where we are,” said Charles Lister, director of the Syria Initiative at the Middle East Institute in Washington, DC. Interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa is racing to rebuild Syria – an estimated $216 billion task – before patience runs out. He inherited a nearly bankrupt state that was plundered by Assad and his cronies, leaving the new regime largely reliant on foreign investment. His strategy has been to bring the country back onto the global stage after decades of isolation, and he is now trying to turn that international momentum into tangible economic gains. “Syria has restored its status into the international community. It has been a transit for the world. We also built diplomatic bridges and we proved to the world that the security of the region has to start in Damascus,” al-Sharaa told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday. The global embrace of al-Sharaa is perhaps best embodied by his warm rapport with US President Donald Trump, who he has met four times since last May. The outcome has been the complete lifting of all US sanctions on Syria, the key to unlocking foreign investment. Turkey, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have driven most foreign investments thus far, estimated by Syria last year at $28 billion. The European Union has committed $2.7 billion in support, and French President Emmanuel Macron signed several new economic, transport and infrastructure agreements during a July visit to Damascus. By one Syria expert’s count, the new government has met with representatives from about 100 countries since taking power. In a display of pragmatism, al-Sharaa even maintains ties with both Russian President Vladimir Putin, a top ally of the former regime, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Syria’s strategic geography The breadth of that engagement reflects Syria’s strategic position. At a time of international discord, supporting Syria’s future has become a rare point of consensus – and the reason largely lies in geography. Syria sits at the heart of the Middle East, connecting Asia and Europe through its Mediterranean ports. It reflects the belief that, just as the Syrian civil war reverberated far beyond its borders – sparking a migration crisis and enabling the rise of ISIS – a stable and prosperous Syria could bolster regional stability, encourage refugee returns and curb extremism. Amid the Iran war, al-Sharaa has leveraged Syria’s strategic location to pitch it as a modern Silk Road, a trade hub that serves as a land bridge alternative to the straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb. A proof of concept is already under way as thousands of tanker trucks loaded with oil from southern Iraq cross through Syria to the Mediterranean port of Baniyas. But for ordinary Syrians, the government’s ambitious plans have yet to show tangible results. Lister says the international community sees a real opportunity in rebuilding Syria’s future, but it will take time. “The reality is that most of these projects are 10-year strategic projects. They’re not going to reduce the price of bread, or immediately bring in more fuel or reduce the cost of fuel in Syria,” he said. Lister says the end of American sanctions has brought in a flurry of new small and medium-sized investment projects that will put people to work more quickly. “It’s those kinds of projects that offer a far greater chance of starting to put the seeds in the ground that lead to an amelioration of the challenges ordinary Syrians face,” he said. “But it’s not going to result in those things being fixed next week. It’s probably going to take another year or two.” ‘Revolutionary’ political capital running out Karam Shaar, a Syrian political economist who runs an advisory firm, estimates that just 5% of the promised deals have made tangible progress. Among the most visible are the renovations of power infrastructure and the Damascus airport by UCC Holding, led by the influential Syrian-Qatari Al-Khayyat brothers. “The economy is undoubtedly recovering. But that’s never the question for the average person. What matters to them is whether their livelihoods are improving,” he told CNN. A Syrian protester, Bassam Al-Ali, complained to Reuters that the government was focused on big-dollar deals rather than cost-of-living improvements. “We do not want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout that costs a million thousand dollars and malls and I don’t know what. Let your people live,” he said, addressing al-Sharaa. “Your people were with you, are still with you now and will remain with you but this will let things explode.” Al-Assil warned that as economic grievances build, the “revolutionary legitimacy” al-Sharaa’s government has accrued could fade away. “Buying patience from people requires allowing them to participate, making them feel that their voices are heard.” The Israel factor But even if the government can close the gap between international investment and everyday economic improvement, it faces another obstacle largely outside its control, one that al-Sharaa directly called out at the UN on Wednesday. “The world is joyed about our return. But Israel is launching attacks against Syria,” he said. “This is at odds with the orientation we’re seeing at the global level.” He estimated Israel has carried out nearly 500 strikes in Syria since he took power. Israel also occupies large parts of southern Syria and Israeli officials have said the military plans to stay there indefinitely. Israel claims it does not trust al-Sharaa and needs a security buffer to prevent terrorism attacks on its soil. War-weary Syria maintains it does not want a conflict with its neighbor. The two sides have been in direct talks since August of last year. Al-Sharaa said Tuesday at an Atlantic Council panel in New York that negotiations “reached 90% of agreements” until Israel withdrew for “different reasons.” Lister says the instability brought on by Israel’s actions is a top concern among investors who ask him about opportunities in Syria. “If the Israelis continue their current posture after their elections (in October), then more and more external investment into Syria is less likely – because they are waving this massive hammer over the head of Damascus,” he said. “This particular issue is just as central to the questions around economic recovery as sanctions, as investment prospects, as small and medium-sized enterprises. Israel is just as important.”

articles.title: Estonia says Russia ordered August arson attack on defence company
articles.summary: Tallinn accuses Moscow of responsibility for the fire at Estonian company Milrem Robotics, a supplier of unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine.
articles.body:
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna has accused Russia of “sabotage” following an August arson attack on a defence company, Milrem Robotics, a claim the Kremlin rejected.

“We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack … in Tallinn was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation,” Tsahkna wrote on X on Tuesday.

He added that the perpetrators of the attack had been apprehended and “no longer pose a threat”, and that Estonia had summoned the Russian ambassador.

“This act of sabotage is part of Russia’s broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine,” he wrote.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov rejected the allegation.

“Such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning. Consequently, we cannot and will not take such statements seriously,” he told reporters.

Estonia, a European Union and NATO member state along the alliance’s eastern flank, has accused Moscow of several hybrid provocations since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Along with its neighbours Latvia and Lithuania, it has ramped up its investment in defence in the years since and remains a staunch ally of Kyiv.

NATO chief Mark Rutte, speaking to journalists after Estonia’s accusation, said that “Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine”.

“But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine, and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine,” he added.

The attack was condemned by several of Estonia’s allies, who also reaffirmed their support for Ukraine.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on X that Paris was in full solidarity with Estonia, adding: “The proliferation of these hostile acts reflects a dangerous headlong rush by Russia – one that will only lead it into a dead end.”

“Russia’s fingerprints are all over” the attack, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys wrote on X, adding that Moscow’s “hostile activities do not stop at Ukraine’s borders”.

Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics added that “more support for Ukraine … will be needed and must be provided”.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson called Estonia’s attribution of the attack “extremely serious”, and said the pattern of the attacks was “directed against Europe as a whole”.

articles.title: Senate Democrats warn Trump administration against Brazil election interference
articles.summary: A trio of Senate Democrats is warning the Trump administration against interference ahead of Brazil’s presidential elections, according to a letter obtained exclusively by The Hill. Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Peter Welch (D-Vt.) in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday warned against U.S. meddling in the elections…
articles.body:
A trio of Senate Democrats is warning the Trump administration against interference ahead of Brazil’s presidential elections, according to a letter obtained exclusively by The Hill.

Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Peter Welch (D-Vt.) in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday warned against U.S. meddling in the elections on Oct. 4.

“Will the Administration commit to recognizing the certified outcome of Brazil’s 2026 democratic elections and to supporting normal diplomatic relations with whichever candidate is freely and fairly chosen by the Brazilian people?” the senators asked, requesting that Rubio respond.

President Trump has relished the victories of his preferred right-wing candidates across Latin America but has so far held back an explicit endorsement in Brazil’s contest.

Still, he has lashed out at the country with tariffs in retaliation for the trial of his political ally: former right-wing, populist President Jair Bolsonaro. The former Brazilian leader was convicted in September 2025 on charges of inciting a coup to stay in power. Trump has recently extended favor to Bolsonaro’s son Flávio, one of 13 candidates running in the October election.

The Democratic senators singled out the State Department’s controversial senior adviser for Western Hemisphere affairs, Darren Beattie, as driving a pattern of aggressive actions against Latin America’s most populous democracy.

“Beattie, a noted far-right extremist and white supremacist, came into this post with a record of public statements signaling an overt ideological commitment to undermining Brazil’s democratic institutions and advancing the interests of the Brazilian far right,” they wrote.

Beattie served in Trump’s first administration but was fired from his position as a speechwriter after it was revealed that he attended a gathering of white supremacists. He founded the right-wing media outlet Revolver News, which reportedly amplified false conspiracy theories about the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. Beattie also reportedly made disparaging comments about people of color online.

Beattie was appointed to his State Department role in February, avoiding Senate confirmation by using the term “senior adviser.” The department’s website says he has “acted as one of the department’s leading voices on Brazil policy as of November 2025.”

Beattie was denied a visa to enter Brazil in March as part of a diplomatic row between Washington and Brasília. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is also running in the October elections, said the visa was denied because the Trump administration blocked Brazil’s health minister from traveling to the U.S.

The Brazilian Foreign Ministry told Reuters at the time that Beattie had omitted or falsified “relevant information regarding the reason for the visit.”

The visa standoff was just one in a pattern of high-profile controversies between Trump and ‌Lula’s government.

Trump welcomed Flávio Bolsonaro into the Oval Office for a short meeting in May, and he then designated Brazil’s two biggest drug gangs as terrorist groups — a move Lula condemned as unacceptable interference in the country’s internal affairs.

Trump has also deployed tariffs against Brazil as retaliation. In July, the U.S. imposed 25 percent tariffs on Brazil over “unfair trade practices” that came after a yearlong investigation initiated in the aftermath of a spat between Trump and Lula .

“Today, rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy, the United States is using diplomatic, economic, and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic U.S. ally and trading partner,” the senators wrote in Monday’s letter.

“These actions reflect a broader and deeply troubling pattern of interference by the Trump Administration in recent electoral processes across Latin America. … This pattern risks not only undermining the integrity of electoral processes in individual countries but also progressively eroding public confidence in democratic processes and institutions across the region.”

articles.title: Rahm Emanuel expresses support for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race
articles.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador Rahm Emanuel insisted the DSA are a separate party, yet he backed Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan's Senate race.
articles.body: AUSTIN, TEXAS — Former U.S. ambassador and lifelong Democrat Rahm Emanuel doubled down on his declaration that democratic socialists don't belong in his party while expressing support for a far-left candidate competing in one of the most highly contested Senate races in the midterms. "Democratic Socialists are a separate party. I'll see you in November," Emanuel told Fox News Digital at the Texas Tribune Festival. Emanuel, who has been mulling a 2028 presidential bid, has been outspoken against the far-left. While he insisted that the Democratic Socialists of America are their own party, they've made their mark on the Democratic ballot, particularly in the 2026 midterms. Democratic socialists have won several congressional Democratic primaries across the country, including three candidates in New York City who were endorsed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, as well as Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Melat Kiros in Colorado and Florida Senate hopeful Angie Dixon. RAHM EMANUEL TOUTS WHAT SEPARATES HIMSELF FROM OTHER DEMS AS HE MULLS 2028 PRESIDENTIAL BID Despite the major gains this election cycle, Emanuel insisted there's no "takeover" of his party. "You think people wanna support defunding the police? You think they wanna support open borders, open prisons? Run on it. I don't, and that's not the party's position," Emanuel said. "Now, we will have healthy debate among progressive and pragmatic wing of the party. That's what a coalition party looks like. But that is it. You had a party convention!" "Swing voters in swing states swing presidential elections. That is it. It's not more complicated. And you better be focused on winning," he added. RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN' Prominent Democratic Socialists like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., have rallied behind Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, though El-Sayed claims not to be a socialist himself. While speaking at the Texas Tribune Festival, Emanuel didn't hesitate to praise Democratic Texas Senate nominee James Talarico, calling him "strong" and admiring Talarico for being "comfortable" about discussing his faith. But when asked by Fox News Digital moments later whether he supports El-Sayed's candidacy, Emanuel initially hedged. RAHM EMANUEL WARNS ‘BERNIE BROS’ COULD SINK DEMOCRATS BY SADDLING MODERATES WITH SOCIALIST AGENDA "Look, I mean, it doesn't matter what I do ... it matters what the Michigan voters think," he told Fox News Digital. "And that's what's gonna determine this in this effort. And I support the Democrats winning the Senate."
